items.subgroup_name: Net operating and capital loss utilization
items.task: Recall the limitations on the use of net operating losses when there is an ownership change.
items.stem: Bristol Ridge, Inc. is a loss corporation with a large net operating loss carryforward. Which event during the last three years is an ownership change that limits use of the carryforward?
options: Two unrelated investors who owned no stock bought 30% and 15% of the stock, and no other shareholder's interest changed
The corporation's founder gave 60% of the stock to her two adult children in equal shares, and no other interest changed
A single investor who already owned 20% of the stock bought another 10%, and no other shareholder's interest changed
Two unrelated investors who owned no stock bought 30% and 25% of the stock, and no other shareholder's interest changed
items.rule_line: An ownership change occurs when the percentage of stock held by 5-percent shareholders rises by more than 50 points over a testing period of up to three years.

why.A: The combined increase is 45 percentage points, which does not exceed the 50-point threshold.
why.B: Family members are aggregated as a single owner under the attribution rules, so there is no increase in ownership by a new shareholder group.
why.C: The increase is only 10 percentage points. The rule needs an increase of more than 50 points in the aggregate.
why.D: An ownership change occurs when 5-percent shareholders increase their combined ownership by more than 50 percentage points within a three-year testing period; 30 + 25 = 55 points.

items.subgroup_name: Net operating and capital loss utilization
items.task: Calculate the amount of a C corporation's net operating loss for a given year and any related carryforward.
items.stem: Tamarack Foods, Inc. had a net operating loss of $200,000 in 2025 and a net operating loss of $300,000 in 2026, and no earlier loss carryovers. Its 2027 taxable income before any net operating loss deduction is $350,000. Assume both losses arose in years beginning after 2020 and can only be carried forward. How much of the 2026 net operating loss remains to be carried to 2028?
items.rule_line: Post-2020 NOLs carry forward only, are used oldest first, and the deduction is limited to 80% of taxable income computed before the NOL deduction.

why.A: Uses the 2026 loss first. Losses are absorbed from the earliest year forward.
why.B: Nets the two losses against each other instead of applying them to 2027 income.
why.C: Ignores the 80% limit and uses losses against all of the taxable income.
why.D: The deduction is limited to 80% of $350,000 = $280,000. Losses are used oldest first: all $200,000 of the 2025 loss, then $80,000 of the 2026 loss. The 2026 loss remaining is $300,000 - $80,000 = $220,000.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / NOL carryforward / Application

items.subgroup_name: Net operating and capital loss utilization
items.task: Calculate the amount of a C corporation's capital loss utilized in the current year and the related carryforward or carryback.
items.stem: Alder Bay Corp. had a net long-term capital loss of $50,000 in 2026 and no capital gains that year. It had no capital gains in 2023 through 2025, so no part of the loss can be carried back. In 2027 it has a short-term capital gain of $20,000, a long-term capital gain of $10,000, and ordinary income of $100,000. It has no other capital loss carryovers. How much of the 2026 capital loss remains to be carried forward after 2027?
items.rule_line: A corporation's capital loss carryover is treated as short-term and offsets all net capital gain; it is never deductible against ordinary income.

why.A: A corporation's capital loss carryover is treated as a short-term loss and offsets any capital gains of the carryover year, both short-term and long-term. It absorbs $20,000 + $10,000 = $30,000, leaving $20,000.
why.B: Offsets only the short-term gain. A corporate carryover is treated as short-term and offsets both kinds of gain.
why.C: Offsets only the long-term gain, which reverses the character rules.
why.D: Assumes no part of the loss is absorbed by the 2027 gains.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Capital loss carryover / Application

items.subgroup_name: Net operating and capital loss utilization
items.task: Recall the limitations on the use of net operating losses when there is an ownership change.
items.stem: Ridge Line Corp. had an ownership change in 2026. It has a net operating loss carryforward of $900,000, all from years beginning after 2020. The value of its stock immediately before the change was $2,000,000 and the long-term tax-exempt rate for the month of the change was 3.5%. Its 2027 taxable income before any net operating loss deduction is $300,000, and the corporate rate is 21%. What is its 2027 federal income tax?
items.rule_line: After an ownership change, annual use of pre-change NOLs is limited to the value of the loss corporation times the long-term tax-exempt rate; the 80% limit also applies.

why.A: Ignores the ownership change limitation and applies only the 80% limit.
why.B: The annual limit is $2,000,000 x 3.5% = $70,000, which is less than the 80% limit ($240,000) and less than the loss carryforward. Taxable income = $300,000 - $70,000 = $230,000; tax = 21% x $230,000 = $48,300.
why.C: Applies the rate to the size of the loss rather than the value of the corporation's stock.
why.D: Allows no deduction for the carryforward. The ownership change limits, but does not eliminate, use of the loss.

items.subgroup_name: Net operating and capital loss utilization
items.task: Calculate the amount of a C corporation's net operating loss for a given year and any related carryforward.
items.stem: Copper Bend Corp., a calendar-year C corporation, had an operating loss of $60,000 in 2026 before considering dividends. It also received $100,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 25% of the stock. Assume the dividends-received deduction is 65% of qualifying dividends when it applies, and that the general limit is 65% of taxable income computed without the deduction. What is its 2026 net operating loss?
items.rule_line: The 65% of taxable income limit on the dividends-received deduction does not apply if the full deduction creates or increases a net operating loss.

why.A: Applies the taxable income limit and reports no loss. The limit does not apply when the full deduction creates a net operating loss.
why.B: Taxable income before the deduction is $100,000 - $60,000 = $40,000. The 65% limit would allow only $26,000, but the limit does not apply if the full deduction would create or increase a net operating loss. The full deduction of $65,000 produces a loss of $25,000.
why.C: Ignores the dividends and the dividends-received deduction.
why.D: Subtracts the deduction from the operating loss without including the dividends in income first.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate a shareholder's tax realized and recognized gain (loss) on the contribution of noncash property to a C corporation, and the C corporation's basis in the property contributed.
items.stem: Hale Rowan transfers land with a basis of $60,000 and a fair market value of $150,000 to a newly formed corporation, Rowan Holdings, Inc., in exchange for stock worth $120,000 and $30,000 in cash. Hale owns all of the stock after the exchange and the land is not encumbered. What is Rowan Holdings' basis in the land?
items.rule_line: In a section 351 transfer, the corporation's basis equals the transferor's basis increased by gain recognized on boot.

why.A: Uses only Hale's basis. The corporation increases the carryover basis by the gain Hale recognizes.
why.B: The exchange qualifies under the control rules. Hale realizes a gain of $90,000 and recognizes the lesser of the boot ($30,000) or the gain: $30,000. The corporation's basis is Hale's basis plus the gain he recognizes: $60,000 + $30,000 = $90,000.
why.C: Uses the value of the stock received rather than the transferor's basis and recognized gain.
why.D: Uses fair market value, which applies only in a taxable exchange.

steps: Recognized gain = lesser of boot 30,000 or gain $90,000 = $30,000

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate a shareholder's tax realized and recognized gain (loss) on the contribution of noncash property to a C corporation, and the C corporation's basis in the property contributed.
items.stem: Rita Vale transfers equipment with an adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 to a new corporation in exchange for all of its stock. The corporation also assumes a $45,000 business loan on the equipment. What gain does Rita recognize on the transfer?
items.rule_line: In a section 351 transfer, liabilities assumed in excess of the transferor's total basis are recognized as gain.

why.A: Assumes nonrecognition applies without exception. Liabilities in excess of basis trigger gain.
why.B: Liabilities assumed ($45,000) exceed her basis ($30,000) in the transferred property, so she recognizes gain equal to the excess: $15,000. Her stock basis is then $30,000 - $45,000 + $15,000 = $0.
why.C: Recognizes the entire liability as gain, ignoring the basis.
why.D: Recognizes the entire built-in gain. Only the excess of liabilities over basis is recognized.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate a shareholder's tax realized and recognized gain (loss) on the contribution of noncash property to a C corporation, and the C corporation's basis in the property contributed.
items.stem: Ana Kaur transfers equipment with an adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $90,000 to Kaur Design, Inc. for 60% of its stock. Ben Ortiz, who transfers no property, receives the other 40% of the stock for services worth $60,000. What gain does Ana recognize on her transfer?
items.rule_line: Stock issued for services is not counted in the 80% control group; if property transferors own less than 80%, the transfer is a taxable exchange.

why.A: Assumes the exchange qualifies for nonrecognition. Control requires the property transferors to own at least 80%.
why.B: Reports her basis as the gain. The gain is the excess of value over basis.
why.C: Stock issued for services does not count toward the 80% control test. Ana, the only transferor of property, owns only 60% immediately after the exchange, so section 351 does not apply. She recognizes the full gain, $90,000 - $30,000 = $60,000.
why.D: Treats the whole amount realized as gain and ignores her basis.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a C corporation and shareholders on a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: Fenwick Tool Corp., which has ample earnings and profits, distributes equipment with an adjusted basis of $90,000 and a fair market value of $60,000 to its sole shareholder, Ella Frank, as a dividend. What are Ella's dividend income and her basis in the equipment?
options: Dividend of $60,000 and a basis of $60,000
Dividend of $90,000 and a basis of $90,000
Dividend of $60,000 and a basis of $90,000
Dividend of $30,000 and a basis of $60,000
items.rule_line: A shareholder is taxed on a property distribution at fair market value and takes that value as basis; the corporation recognizes no loss.

why.A: A corporation recognizes no loss on a distribution of property that has declined in value. The shareholder's dividend and basis are the property's fair market value, $60,000.
why.B: Uses the corporation's adjusted basis. A shareholder is taxed on and takes basis equal to fair market value.
why.C: Takes the dividend at fair market value but carries over the corporation's basis. The shareholder's basis is fair market value.
why.D: Treats only the decline in value as the dividend.

steps: Shareholder's basis = 60,000; corporation's loss of 30,000 is not recognized

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a C corporation and shareholders on a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: Granite Bluff Corp., which has ample earnings and profits, distributes land with a basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $120,000, subject to a $50,000 mortgage that the shareholder assumes, to its sole shareholder. The corporate rate is 21%. What is the amount of the shareholder's dividend, and what federal income tax does the corporation owe on the gain from the distribution?
options: Dividend of $120,000; corporate tax of $18,900
Dividend of $70,000; corporate tax of $18,900
Dividend of $70,000; corporate tax of $8,400
Dividend of $90,000; corporate tax of $18,900
items.rule_line: A property distribution triggers corporate gain on fair market value; the shareholder's dividend equals fair market value less liabilities assumed.

why.A: Ignores the mortgage. The distribution is reduced by the liability the shareholder assumes.
why.B: The corporation recognizes gain of $120,000 - $30,000 = $90,000, taxed at 21% = $18,900. The amount distributed is fair market value reduced by the liability assumed: $70,000.
why.C: Reduces the corporation's gain by the mortgage. The gain is measured against fair market value, not net equity.
why.D: Treats the corporation's gain as the shareholder's dividend.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Nonliquidating distribution / Application

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a C corporation and shareholders on a liquidating distribution, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: Sam Prowse owns all of the stock of Prowse Supply, Inc., with a stock basis of $50,000. In a complete liquidation in 2026 he receives $60,000 in cash and land worth $90,000. What capital gain does Sam recognize on the liquidation?
items.rule_line: In a complete liquidation the shareholder recognizes gain or loss equal to fair market value received less stock basis.

why.A: Counts only the cash. Property received in a complete liquidation is included at fair market value.
why.B: Counts only the land. The cash is also part of the amount realized.
why.C: The shareholder's gain is the amount realized ($60,000 + $90,000 = $150,000) less stock basis ($50,000): $100,000. His basis in the land will be $90,000.
why.D: Ignores the shareholder's stock basis.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Liquidating distribution / Application

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a C corporation and shareholders on a liquidating distribution, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: Windmere Corp. has two assets: a building worth $200,000 with an adjusted basis of $80,000, and $100,000 of cash. It has no liabilities other than its 2026 income tax. It liquidates completely, distributing the building and its remaining cash to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $150,000. Assume the corporate rate is 21% and the corporation has no other income or deductions. What gain does the shareholder recognize?
items.rule_line: In a liquidation the corporation is taxed on gain as if it sold its assets at fair market value; the shareholder's gain is net of that tax.

why.A: Uses the corporation's gain as the shareholder's gain instead of the shareholder's own amount realized less stock basis.
why.B: The corporation recognizes gain of $200,000 - $80,000 = $120,000 and pays tax of $25,200 from its cash. The shareholder receives the building ($200,000) plus $74,800 of cash, or $274,800, and recognizes gain of $274,800 - $150,000 = $124,800.
why.C: Ignores the corporate tax on the gain from the deemed sale. The tax reduces what the shareholder receives.
why.D: Ignores the shareholder's stock basis.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate the amount and treatment of the cash distributions to shareholders in excess of a C corporation's current and accumulated earnings and profits (E&P).
items.stem: Ridgemont Corp. began 2026 with accumulated earnings and profits of $150,000. It has a current-year earnings and profits deficit of $40,000 for 2026 that accrued evenly through the year. On June 30 it distributed $140,000 in cash to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $90,000. How much of the distribution is a dividend?
items.rule_line: With a current deficit and positive accumulated E&P, the deficit is prorated to the distribution date to measure accumulated E&P available for dividends.

why.A: Subtracts more than the full-year deficit from accumulated earnings and profits.
why.B: Subtracts the deficit from the distribution instead of adjusting accumulated earnings and profits.
why.C: Subtracts the full-year deficit. The deficit is prorated to the distribution date.
why.D: When the current year has a deficit, accumulated earnings and profits at the distribution date is reduced by the deficit prorated to that date: $150,000 - (6/12 x $40,000) = $130,000. The distribution is a dividend to that extent, so $130,000; the remaining $10,000 is a return of basis.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Distributions in excess of E&P / Application

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Calculate the amount and treatment of the cash distributions to shareholders in excess of a C corporation's current and accumulated earnings and profits (E&P).
items.stem: Pinegate Corp. distributed $135,000 in cash to its sole shareholder in 2026. The corporation had current earnings and profits of $70,000 and accumulated earnings and profits of $20,000. The shareholder's stock basis was $30,000. What capital gain does the shareholder recognize?
items.rule_line: Distributions are dividends to the extent of E&P, then a return of basis, then capital gain.

why.A: Assumes the entire distribution is covered by earnings and profits or basis.
why.B: Dividends come first from current and accumulated earnings and profits ($70,000 + $20,000 = $90,000). The next $30,000 is a tax-free return of basis, reducing basis to $0, and the remaining $15,000 is capital gain.
why.C: Treats all of the distribution above earnings and profits as gain without first reducing basis.
why.D: Ignores earnings and profits and taxes only the excess over basis.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Distributions in excess of E&P / Application

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and a C corporation
items.task: Review loan documents and supporting documentation to determine the tax implications of a loan between a shareholder and C corporation, including imputed interest.
items.stem: On January 1, 2026, Orchard Supply, Inc. lends its sole shareholder, Dev Patel, $300,000 on a demand note that bears no interest. Assume the applicable rate for 2026 is 4.0% and the loan remains outstanding for the whole year. Which statement describes the 2026 tax effect?
options: Neither the corporation nor Dev has any income, because no interest is charged and the note is not repaid until it is called
The corporation reports no income, and Dev reports $12,000 of interest income received from the corporation on the loan
The corporation reports $12,000 of interest income, and Dev is treated as receiving a $12,000 dividend
The corporation reports $300,000 as a distribution, because the entire loan principal is treated as a dividend to Dev
items.rule_line: A below-market loan from a corporation to a shareholder creates imputed interest income to the corporation and a deemed dividend to the shareholder.

why.A: Interest is imputed on a below-market loan even when no payment is made.
why.B: The corporation is the lender, so it reports the imputed interest; the shareholder is the borrower.
why.C: A below-market loan between a corporation and a shareholder is recharacterized: the corporation is treated as paying a dividend to the shareholder, who pays the interest back.
why.D: The loan is not a distribution. Only the foregone interest is treated as a transfer.

items.task: Recall the requirements for filing a consolidated federal Form 1120 – U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return.
items.stem: Which group of corporations may file a consolidated federal income tax return?
options: A domestic parent that owns 60% of the voting power and 90% of the value of a domestic subsidiary
Two domestic corporations that are each owned 100% by the same individual shareholder
A domestic parent that owns 100% of a foreign subsidiary that has no U.S. business operations
A domestic parent that owns at least 80% of the vote and value of a domestic subsidiary
items.rule_line: A consolidated return requires an affiliated group of includible corporations linked through 80% vote-and-value ownership to a common parent.

why.A: Both the vote test and the value test must reach 80%.
why.B: A brother-sister group is not an affiliated group; the common parent must be a corporation.
why.C: Foreign corporations are generally not includible corporations in a consolidated return.
why.D: An affiliated group requires a common parent that owns stock with at least 80% of the total voting power and at least 80% of the total value of each includible corporation.

items.task: Calculate taxable income for a consolidated federal Form 1120 – U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return, including elimination of intercompany transactions.
items.stem: Parent Corp. and its wholly owned subsidiary, Sub Corp., file a consolidated return. Excluding the transaction below, Parent's taxable income is $500,000 and Sub's is $300,000. During 2026 Parent sold inventory that cost $70,000 to Sub for $100,000. By year end Sub had resold 40% of that inventory to unrelated customers for $52,000 and still held the rest. What is the group's consolidated taxable income for 2026?
items.rule_line: Intercompany gain is deferred and taken into account when the property leaves the group (matching rule).

why.A: Subtracts Sub's gain instead of adding it.
why.B: Ignores the intercompany sale and the resale entirely.
why.C: Leaves out Parent's intercompany gain entirely. The gain is taken into account as the inventory is resold outside the group.
why.D: Parent's intercompany gain ($100,000 - $70,000 = $30,000) is taken into account as Sub sells to outsiders: 40% x $30,000 = $12,000. Sub's gain on the resold portion is $52,000 - (40% x $100,000) = $12,000. Consolidated taxable income = $500,000 + $300,000 + $12,000 + $12,000 = $824,000.

steps: Parent's gain taken into account = 40% x $30,000 = $12,000

items.task: Calculate taxable income for a consolidated federal Form 1120 – U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return, including elimination of intercompany transactions.
items.stem: Parent Corp. and Sub Corp. file a consolidated return for 2026. Parent has separate taxable income of $300,000 and Sub has a separate net operating loss of $60,000. What is the group's 2026 federal income tax at 21%?
items.rule_line: Consolidated taxable income combines each member's income and loss for the year.

why.A: Taxes only the amount of Sub's loss.
why.B: Counts Sub's loss twice.
why.C: Applies an unrelated 80% factor to the combined income.
why.D: In a consolidated return, members' income and losses are combined, so Sub's loss offsets Parent's income: ($300,000 - $60,000) x 21% = $50,400.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Consolidated taxable income / Application

items.task: Calculate taxable income for a consolidated federal Form 1120 – U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return, including elimination of intercompany transactions.
items.stem: Parent Corp. and its wholly owned subsidiary, Sub Corp., file a consolidated return. In 2026 Parent has $300,000 of operating income, Sub has $200,000 of operating income, and Sub pays Parent a $80,000 cash dividend. Neither has other items. What is the group's consolidated taxable income?
items.rule_line: Distributions between members of a consolidated group are eliminated, so they do not increase consolidated taxable income.

why.A: Counts only Parent's operating income.
why.B: Counts only Parent's income and the dividend.
why.C: Intercompany dividends are eliminated in consolidation, so the $80,000 dividend is excluded from consolidated taxable income. The total is $300,000 + $200,000 = $500,000.
why.D: Includes the dividend as income to Parent. Intercompany dividends are excluded.

steps: Consolidated taxable income = 300,000 + 200,000 = $500,000; the dividend is eliminated
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Consolidated taxable income / Application

items.task: Explain the sourcing of income for a U.S. corporation with foreign operations.
items.stem: Sable Systems, Inc., a domestic corporation, earned the following items in 2026. Which item is foreign source income?
options: Fees for consulting services performed by its employees in Germany
Interest received from a domestic corporation on a bond issued to Sable
Dividends received from a domestic corporation whose stock Sable holds as an investment
Rent from a U.S. tenant leasing a building that Sable owns in Ohio
items.rule_line: Services income is sourced where performed; interest and dividends by the payor's residence; rents and royalties by the location or use of the property.

why.A: Compensation for services is sourced where the services are performed, so services performed in Germany produce foreign source income.
why.B: Interest is sourced by the residence of the payer, so interest from a domestic obligor is U.S. source.
why.C: Dividends are sourced by the payor's place of incorporation, so a dividend from a domestic corporation is U.S. source.
why.D: Rent from real property is sourced where the property is located, which is in the United States.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Sourcing — US corp foreign ops / Remembering & Understanding

items.task: Explain the sourcing of income for a foreign corporation with U.S. operations, including consideration of federal tax withholding requirements.
items.stem: Nordica AG, a foreign corporation with no U.S. trade or business, receives $100,000 of royalties in 2026 from a U.S. company for the use of a patent in the United States. There is no applicable income tax treaty. Which statement is correct?
options: The U.S. payor withholds 21% of the net royalty after allowing deductions, because a foreign corporation pays the corporate rate
The U.S. payor must withhold 30% of the gross royalty, and that withholding satisfies the foreign corporation's U.S. income tax
No withholding is required because the foreign corporation has no U.S. office
The U.S. payor withholds 30% only if the foreign corporation files a return to claim the income as effectively connected
items.rule_line: Passive U.S.-source income paid to a foreign corporation is subject to 30% withholding on the gross amount unless a treaty reduces the rate.

why.A: Withholding is at a flat 30% of gross amounts. Deductions are not allowed against this income.
why.B: Fixed or determinable annual or periodical income of a foreign person is taxed at a flat 30% of gross, collected by withholding.
why.C: The royalty is U.S. source and is subject to withholding without regard to whether the payee has a U.S. office.
why.D: Effectively connected income is reported on a return and is not subject to the 30% gross withholding. Nordica has no U.S. trade or business, so this royalty is not effectively connected, and filing a return does not change the withholding.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Sourcing — foreign corp US ops / Application

items.task: Explain the concept of a controlled foreign corporation (CFC) and the impact on a U.S. corporation's taxable income.
items.stem: Which foreign corporation is a controlled foreign corporation for 2026? Each U.S. person listed owns stock directly and is unrelated to the others.
options: Corporation X, owned 8% each by seven unrelated U.S. persons and 44% by foreign persons
Corporation Y, owned 45% by U.S. person A and 55% by foreign persons unrelated to A
Corporation W, owned 30% by U.S. person A, 25% by U.S. person B, and 45% by foreign owners
Corporation Z, owned exactly 50% by U.S. person A and exactly 50% by foreign persons
items.rule_line: A foreign corporation is a CFC if U.S. shareholders (each owning 10% or more) own more than 50% of its vote or value.

why.A: No U.S. person owns 10% or more, so none is a U.S. shareholder for the control test.
why.B: U.S. shareholders own only 45%, which is not more than 50%.
why.C: U.S. shareholders each own at least 10% and together own more than 50% of the vote or value: 30% + 25% = 55%.
why.D: The test requires more than 50%. Exactly 50% ownership by U.S. shareholders is not enough.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / CFC / Application

items.task: Explain the concept of permanent establishment for a corporation and the activities that would create it.
items.stem: Norwood Ltd. is a foreign corporation resident in a country with which the United States has an income tax treaty that follows the OECD model. Which activity in the United States most likely creates a permanent establishment?
options: Using a leased warehouse solely to store and deliver goods that it owns to its customers in the United States
Maintaining an office solely to purchase goods for its own use and for resale by it in its home country
Keeping a stock of goods solely for processing by another enterprise in the United States for the corporation
Maintaining a fixed office where its employees negotiate and habitually conclude sales contracts
items.rule_line: A permanent establishment is a fixed place of business, or a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts; storage, purchasing, and other preparatory activities are excluded.

why.A: Storage or delivery of goods solely for the enterprise is a listed exception under the model treaty.
why.B: A fixed place used only for purchasing is a preparatory or auxiliary activity that does not create a permanent establishment.
why.C: Stock held solely for processing by another enterprise is excluded from permanent establishment status.
why.D: A fixed place of business through which the enterprise carries on business, including habitual conclusion of contracts, is a permanent establishment.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group A / Permanent establishment / Remembering & Understanding

items.task: Explain the difference between a foreign branch and foreign subsidiary with respect to federal income taxation to a U.S. corporation.
items.stem: Crestview Corp., a domestic C corporation with substantial U.S. income, plans to start a business in a foreign country and expects to lose $200,000 in the first year. Which structure allows Crestview to deduct that first-year loss against its U.S. income currently?
options: Operating through a foreign branch, because the branch's loss is part of Crestview's own taxable income
Operating through a wholly owned foreign subsidiary corporation, because a parent may deduct a subsidiary's losses
Operating through a wholly owned foreign subsidiary that files a consolidated return with Crestview
Operating through a foreign subsidiary and deducting the loss when the subsidiary's stock is later sold at a gain
items.rule_line: A foreign branch is part of the domestic corporation, so its losses offset U.S. income; a foreign subsidiary's losses stay in the subsidiary.

why.A: A branch is not a separate taxpayer, so its results are included in the domestic corporation's return.
why.B: A foreign subsidiary is a separate corporation and its losses stay within it; the parent cannot deduct them.
why.C: Foreign corporations are generally not includible in a domestic consolidated return.
why.D: A subsidiary's operating losses do not flow to the parent, and a later gain on the stock does not create a current deduction.

items.task: Calculate U.S. and foreign source income given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Quarry Rock Co., a domestic corporation, manufactures machinery in Ohio and sells it to customers in Mexico. Title passes to the customers in Mexico. Gross income from these sales in 2026 is $400,000. All of its production assets are in Ohio. What amount of the gross income is foreign source?
items.rule_line: Income from inventory a taxpayer produces in the United States and sells abroad is sourced solely by the location of its production assets; the title passage rule applies only to purchased inventory.

why.A: Income from inventory produced in the United States and sold abroad is sourced solely on production activity. All production assets are in Ohio, so none of the income is foreign source, even though title passes in Mexico.
why.B: Applies a 25% foreign share, which is not part of any sourcing rule for produced inventory.
why.C: Splits the income equally between production and the place where title passes. That 50-50 split is not part of the current rules for produced inventory; sourcing depends only on production activity.
why.D: Sources all of the income where title passes. The title passage rule applies to inventory the taxpayer purchased, not inventory it produced.

steps: Inventory produced in the United States and sold abroad: source = location of production assets (Reg. 1.863-3(b))
All production assets are in Ohio, so 100% of the $400,000 is U.S. source
items.law_note: Corrected in the 2026-09-29 review: the draft used a 50-50 method (answer $200,000), but current Reg. §1.863-3(b) allocates section 863(b) sales income solely by production activity, and the 50-50 method is not in the current regulation.

items.task: Calculate U.S. and foreign source income given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Delta Manufacturing, Inc. has $300,000 of U.S. source gross income and $200,000 of foreign source gross income. It has $70,000 of deductions definitely related to the foreign income, $100,000 definitely related to the U.S. income, and $60,000 of shared expenses that are apportioned on the basis of gross income. What is its foreign source taxable income?
items.rule_line: Deductions are first allocated to the income they relate to; shared deductions are apportioned by a reasonable basis such as gross income.

why.A: Foreign source gross income is $200,000/$500,000 = 40% of the total, so 40% of the shared expenses, $24,000, are apportioned to foreign income. Foreign taxable income = $200,000 - $70,000 - $24,000 = $106,000.
why.B: Ignores the shared expenses. They must be apportioned between the two sources.
why.C: Leaves out the deductions definitely related to foreign income.
why.D: Uses foreign gross income without any deductions.

items.task: Explain the sourcing of income for a foreign corporation with U.S. operations, including consideration of federal tax withholding requirements.
items.stem: Baltic Holdings, a foreign corporation resident in a country with no treaty relief, operates a U.S. branch. In 2026 its effectively connected taxable income is $1,000,000, taxed at the 21% corporate rate, and its effectively connected earnings and profits equal that income after the regular tax. During 2026 its U.S. net equity increased by $200,000. What branch profits tax does it owe at the 30% statutory rate?
items.rule_line: The branch profits tax is 30% of the dividend equivalent amount: effectively connected E&P adjusted for changes in U.S. net equity.

why.A: Applies the tax to the reinvested amount rather than the earnings not reinvested.
why.B: Subtracts the increase in U.S. net equity twice.
why.C: Applies the 21% corporate rate to the dividend equivalent amount.
why.D: Effectively connected E&P is $1,000,000 - $210,000 = $790,000. The dividend equivalent amount is reduced by the $200,000 increase in U.S. net equity: $590,000. The branch profits tax is 30% x $590,000 = $177,000.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from nonliquidating distributions of noncash property.
items.stem: Rob Yates, an S corporation shareholder, began 2026 with a stock basis of $55,000. His share of the corporation's 2026 items was ordinary income of $42,000, tax-exempt interest of $6,500, a charitable contribution of $3,000, and nondeductible expenses of $2,400. He also received distributions of $25,000. What is his stock basis at the end of 2026?
items.rule_line: S corporation stock basis increases for income items and decreases for distributions, then for nondeductible expenses and losses.

why.A: Leaves out the ordinary income, which increases basis.
why.B: Leaves out the tax-exempt interest, which increases basis even though it is not taxed.
why.C: Subtracts the nondeductible expenses twice.
why.D: Basis rises for income items ($42,000 + $6,500), falls for distributions ($25,000), and then falls for nondeductible expenses and deductions ($3,000 + $2,400): $55,000 + $48,500 - $25,000 - $5,400 = $73,100.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group B / Stock basis — distribution / Application

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from nonliquidating distributions of noncash property.
items.stem: Maya Fenn owns all the stock of an S corporation. Her stock basis at the start of 2026 was $30,000, and she has no debt basis. For 2026 the corporation had an ordinary loss of $20,000 and made a cash distribution to her of $25,000. How much of the 2026 loss is suspended because of the basis limitation?
items.rule_line: In an S corporation, basis is reduced by distributions before it is reduced by losses.

why.A: Distributions reduce basis before losses. Basis after the distribution is $30,000 - $25,000 = $5,000, so only $5,000 of the $20,000 loss is deductible, and $15,000 is suspended.
why.B: Suspends the entire loss and ignores the remaining basis after the distribution.
why.C: Reports the distribution amount instead of the suspended loss.
why.D: Reports the starting stock basis instead of the suspended loss.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group B / Stock basis — distribution / Application

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's debt basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from loans made by a shareholder to an S corporation.
items.stem: Lena Ong is the sole shareholder of an S corporation with a 2026 ordinary loss of $120,000. Her stock basis is $20,000. She made a $30,000 cash loan to the corporation evidenced by a written note, and she personally guaranteed a separate $50,000 bank loan to the corporation but has not paid anything under the guarantee. How much of the loss may she deduct in 2026, ignoring at-risk and passive limits?
items.rule_line: A shareholder's loss deduction is limited to stock basis plus basis in direct loans to the corporation; guarantees do not count until paid.

why.A: Subtracts her stock basis from the loan amount.
why.B: Counts only stock basis. Direct shareholder loans also give her debt basis.
why.C: Counts only the direct loan and leaves out her stock basis.
why.D: The loss is limited to stock basis plus debt basis: $20,000 + $30,000 = $50,000. Her guarantee of a bank loan does not create basis until she pays under it.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and an S corporation
items.task: Calculate a shareholder's tax realized and recognized gain (loss) on the contribution of noncash property to an S corporation, and the S corporation's basis in the property contributed.
items.stem: Kai Nguyen transfers a building with an adjusted basis of $80,000 and a fair market value of $200,000 to a newly formed S corporation in exchange for all of its stock. The corporation assumes a $90,000 mortgage on the building. What is the S corporation's basis in the building?
items.rule_line: Under section 357(c) the transferor recognizes gain equal to liabilities over basis, and the corporation's basis is increased by that gain.

why.A: Uses the gain recognized as the corporation's basis.
why.B: Subtracts the gain from basis instead of adding it.
why.C: Uses only Kai's basis. The corporation's basis is increased by the gain he recognizes.
why.D: The liability ($90,000) exceeds Kai's basis ($80,000), so he recognizes gain of $10,000. The corporation's basis is his basis increased by the gain recognized: $80,000 + $10,000 = $90,000.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from contributions of noncash property, including an S corporation's assumption of debt on the contributed property.
items.stem: Iris Pak transfers property with an adjusted basis of $60,000 and a fair market value of $200,000 to a new S corporation in exchange for all of its stock. The corporation assumes a $40,000 liability on the property. What is Iris's basis in her stock?
items.rule_line: Stock basis in a section 351 exchange equals the basis of property transferred, less liabilities assumed and boot received, plus gain recognized.

why.A: The liability is less than her basis, so no gain is recognized. Stock basis equals the basis of the property transferred less the liability assumed: $60,000 - $40,000 = $20,000.
why.B: Ignores the liability the corporation assumes, which reduces stock basis.
why.C: Uses the net value of the property rather than the transferor's basis.
why.D: Uses fair market value. Stock basis in a nonrecognition exchange is carryover basis.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and an S corporation
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both an S corporation and shareholders on a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: Tern Dunes, Inc., an S corporation with one shareholder, distributes land with an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 to the shareholder in 2026. The shareholder's stock basis before the distribution is $50,000. How much gain from the distribution is reported by the shareholder?
items.rule_line: An S corporation recognizes gain on distributed appreciated property, which passes through and increases the shareholder's basis before the distribution reduces it.

why.A: An S corporation recognizes gain on a property distribution as if it sold the property at fair market value, and the gain passes through: $100,000 - $20,000 = $80,000. The shareholder's basis then rises by the gain and falls by the value distributed.
why.B: Reports the full value of the land as gain and ignores the corporation's basis.
why.C: Adds the land's basis to its value.
why.D: Adds the shareholder's stock basis to the land's value.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and an S corporation
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both an S corporation and shareholders on a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: An S corporation distributes land with an adjusted basis of $90,000 and a fair market value of $60,000 to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis before the distribution is $100,000. What is the shareholder's stock basis after the distribution?
items.rule_line: A property distribution by an S corporation reduces the shareholder's stock basis by the property's fair market value; no loss is recognized.

why.A: Reduces basis by the corporation's basis in the land. The reduction is the property's fair market value.
why.B: The corporation recognizes no loss on the distribution, and the shareholder's basis is reduced by the fair market value of the property distributed: $100,000 - $60,000 = $40,000.
why.C: Reduces basis only by the built-in loss on the land.
why.D: Assumes property distributions do not reduce stock basis.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and an S corporation
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both an S corporation and shareholders on a liquidating distribution, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: Cedar Wick, Inc., an S corporation, purchased land years ago for $150,000. The land is now worth $100,000. In a complete liquidation the corporation distributes the land and $50,000 of cash pro rata to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $200,000. The corporation recognizes the loss on the land. Which statement correctly describes the result?
options: The corporation recognizes no loss on the land, and the shareholder recognizes a $50,000 capital loss on the stock
A $50,000 section 1231 loss passes through to the shareholder, and the liquidation produces no gain or loss on the stock
A $50,000 section 1231 loss passes through, and the shareholder also recognizes a $50,000 capital loss on the stock
The corporation's $50,000 loss is disallowed because the distribution is made to a related person, so basis remains $200,000
items.rule_line: In a liquidation the S corporation recognizes gain or loss on distributed property, and the pass-through changes stock basis before the shareholder computes gain or loss on the stock.

why.A: A liquidating S corporation recognizes losses on distributed property, subject only to related-party and built-in loss limits that do not apply here.
why.B: The corporation's $50,000 section 1231 loss passes through and reduces stock basis to $150,000; the shareholder receives $150,000 in total, so the stock yields no further gain or loss.
why.C: That counts the same economic loss twice. The pass-through loss reduces the stock basis, leaving no capital loss.
why.D: The related-person disallowance applies to non-pro rata distributions and disqualified property. A pro rata distribution of purchased land is not covered.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and an S corporation
items.task: Calculate the allocation of S corporation income (loss) after the sale of a shareholder's ownership interest in the S corporation for tax purposes.
items.stem: Sun Bay, Inc., a calendar-year S corporation, earned ordinary income of $720,000 for 2026, ratably through the year. Zoe Farr owned 50% of the stock from January 1 until she sold all of her shares on May 10, 2026. The corporation made no election to close its books. Assume the 130 days from January 1 through May 10 (including the transfer date) are counted for Zoe. What share of the income is allocated to Zoe?
items.rule_line: Absent a closing-of-the-books election, S corporation items are allocated per share per day, with the selling shareholder treated as owning the shares through the day of sale.

why.A: Prorates by whole months instead of by days.
why.B: Excludes the day of the sale. The shareholder who sells is treated as owning the shares through the transfer date.
why.C: Without a closing election the income is allocated per day, and the selling shareholder is treated as owning the stock through the day of the sale: $720,000 x 130/365 x 50% = $128,219.
why.D: Allocates the full year's income to Zoe even though she sold her shares in May.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a shareholder and an S corporation
items.task: Calculate the allocation of S corporation income (loss) after the sale of a shareholder's ownership interest in the S corporation for tax purposes.
items.stem: Sun Bay, Inc., a calendar-year S corporation, earned ordinary income of $600,000 from January 1 through May 10, 2026 (Zoe's 50% holding period, including the sale date) and $120,000 from May 11 through December 31. Zoe sold all of her 50% interest on May 10. All affected shareholders consent to an election to close the books at the sale. By how much does the election increase the income allocated to Zoe compared with allocating the year's $720,000 per day? Assume 130 of 365 days fall on or before May 10.
items.rule_line: A closing-of-the-books election allocates income by actual results to the termination date instead of by day, and benefits a seller when income is front-loaded.

why.A: Uses 75% of the per-day amount.
why.B: This is the per-day allocation, not the increase from the election.
why.C: Uses half of Zoe's closing-of-the-books share.
why.D: With the election Zoe's share is 50% x $600,000 = $300,000. Without it she is allocated 50% x $720,000 x 130/365 = $128,219. The difference is $171,781.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from nonliquidating distributions of noncash property.
items.stem: Kay Sato owns 40% of an S corporation with a stock basis of $30,000 at the start of 2026. For 2026 the corporation had ordinary income of $50,000, received $100,000 of life insurance proceeds on the death of an officer (tax-exempt), and paid $8,000 of nondeductible premiums on that policy. Kay received a $20,000 distribution. What is her stock basis at year end?
items.rule_line: Tax-exempt income increases S corporation stock basis; nondeductible expenses and distributions decrease it.

why.A: Leaves out the tax-exempt life insurance proceeds, which increase basis.
why.B: Deducts all of the premiums instead of her 40% share.
why.C: Deducts her share of the premiums twice.
why.D: Her 40% shares of income ($20,000) and tax-exempt proceeds ($40,000) increase basis; the distribution ($20,000) and her share of nondeductible premiums ($3,200) decrease it: $66,800.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from contributions of noncash property, including an S corporation's assumption of debt on the contributed property.
items.stem: Ned Rowe owns stock in an S corporation and has $12,000 of losses suspended from prior years because his stock and debt basis were $0. In 2026 he contributes $20,000 of additional capital to the corporation, and the corporation has a $15,000 ordinary loss for the year. Assume no other basis items. How much of his losses remains suspended at the end of 2026?
items.rule_line: Losses are deductible up to stock and debt basis; excess losses carry forward and are used when basis is restored.

why.A: His basis becomes $20,000. The total of the current loss ($15,000) and the suspended loss ($12,000) is $27,000, but only $20,000 can be deducted, leaving $7,000 suspended.
why.B: Assumes the entire prior suspended loss remains. The added basis can absorb suspended losses after the current loss.
why.C: Keeps only the current-year loss suspended, which does not match how the basis is used.
why.D: Allows no deduction, ignoring the new $20,000 of basis.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's debt basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from loans made by a shareholder to an S corporation.
items.stem: Ora Lindqvist owns 100% of an S corporation that expects a $30,000 loss during 2026. Her stock basis is $5,000 and she has $25,000 of cash. Which action taken during 2026 gives her enough basis to deduct the full loss?
options: Guarantee a $25,000 bank loan to the S corporation without paying anything under the guarantee
Lend the $25,000 to her wholly owned C corporation, which lends the same amount to the S corporation
Lend the $25,000 directly to the S corporation in exchange for a written note
Lend the $25,000 to the S corporation on January 2 of the following year in exchange for a written note
items.rule_line: Debt basis arises from a direct loan by the shareholder to the S corporation, made before year end; guarantees and indirect loans do not qualify.

why.A: A guarantee does not create basis until the shareholder pays under it.
why.B: An indirect loan through another entity does not create basis in the S corporation debt for the shareholder.
why.C: A direct loan from the shareholder creates debt basis, which together with stock basis supports the loss.
why.D: The loan must be made before the end of the year in which the loss is deducted to give basis for that year.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a partner's basis in a partnership for tax purposes resulting from contributions of noncash property, including a partnership's assumption of debt on the contributed property.
items.stem: Amir contributes $50,000 in cash and equipment with an adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $80,000 to a partnership for a 40% interest. The partnership assumes a $20,000 loan on the equipment. After the contribution the partnership's liabilities total $100,000 (including the assumed loan), and Amir's share of them is 40%. What is Amir's basis in his partnership interest?
items.rule_line: Outside basis = cash and property basis contributed, less liabilities assumed by the partnership, plus the partner's share of partnership liabilities.

why.A: Ignores the increase for his share of partnership liabilities.
why.B: Uses only the basis of the property and cash contributed.
why.C: Applies his percentage only to the liabilities other than the loan the partnership assumed.
why.D: Basis starts with cash and property basis ($50,000 + $30,000 = $80,000). Relief of his $20,000 liability reduces it, and his $40,000 share of partnership liabilities increases it: $80,000 - $20,000 + $40,000 = $100,000.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Partner basis — contribution / Application

items.task: Calculate the impact on a partner's basis in a partnership for tax purposes resulting from nonliquidating distributions of noncash property.
items.stem: Uma Reyes began 2026 with a partnership basis of $60,000. Her share of 2026 items was ordinary income of $40,000, tax-exempt interest of $5,000, and a charitable contribution of $3,000. Her share of partnership liabilities increased by $12,000, and she received a cash distribution of $30,000. What is her basis at year end?
items.rule_line: Partnership interest basis increases for income, contributions and liability share, and decreases for distributions, losses and nondeductible items.

why.A: Omits the increase in her share of partnership liabilities.
why.B: Omits tax-exempt interest, which increases basis.
why.C: Basis increases for income and tax-exempt interest ($45,000) and the liability increase ($12,000), then decreases for the distribution ($30,000) and the charitable contribution ($3,000): $84,000.
why.D: Omits the reduction for her share of the charitable contribution.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Partner basis — distribution / Application

items.task: Calculate the impact on a partner's basis in a partnership for tax purposes resulting from nonliquidating distributions of noncash property.
items.stem: Nia Torres has a basis of $12,000 in her partnership interest. In 2026 the partnership repaid loans so that her share of partnership liabilities decreased by $30,000. In the same year she guaranteed a new partnership loan, which increased her share of liabilities by $20,000, and the partnership distributed $10,000 in cash to her. She has no other basis adjustments. What gain does she recognize?
items.rule_line: A net decrease in a partner's share of liabilities is a deemed cash distribution; gain arises to the extent total cash distributions exceed basis.

why.A: Increases and decreases in her share of liabilities are netted. The net decrease is $30,000 - $20,000 = $10,000, treated as a cash distribution. With the actual $10,000, the deemed and actual distributions total $20,000, which exceeds her basis of $12,000 by $8,000.
why.B: Counts only the actual cash distribution and ignores the net liability decrease.
why.C: Reports the total deemed and actual distributions as gain without subtracting her basis.
why.D: Ignores the increase in her share of liabilities, which nets against the decrease.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Partner basis — distribution / Application

items.task: Calculate the impact on a partner's basis in a partnership for tax purposes resulting from recourse and nonrecourse partnership debt incurred during the current year, including loans made by a partner to a partnership.
items.stem: A partnership borrows $300,000 to buy a building. Partners A, B and C share profits 50%, 30% and 20%. A is a limited partner. Consider two loan structures. In the first, the loan is nonrecourse with no partner personally liable and there is no minimum gain and no built-in gain property. In the second, the loan is recourse, and B alone guarantees it with no right of reimbursement. By how much is A's basis increase under the first structure greater than under the second?
items.rule_line: Nonrecourse debt is shared by profit percentages; recourse debt is allocated to the partner who bears the economic risk of loss.

why.A: Uses C's profit percentage, which is not A's share.
why.B: Uses B's profit percentage, which is not A's share.
why.C: Splits the loan equally among the three partners.
why.D: For the nonrecourse loan the liability is shared by profit percentages, giving A 50% x $300,000 = $150,000. For the recourse loan only B bears the economic risk of loss, so A's share is $0. The difference is $150,000.

steps: Recourse guaranteed by B alone: A's share = $0

items.task: Calculate the impact on a partner's basis in a partnership for tax purposes resulting from recourse and nonrecourse partnership debt incurred during the current year, including loans made by a partner to a partnership.
items.stem: Ola Park has a basis of $10,000 in her general partnership interest. In 2026 the partnership repays $60,000 of a recourse loan, and her share of that reduction is 30%. She has no other basis adjustments and receives no other distribution. What gain does she recognize?
items.rule_line: A partner's share of a liability decrease is a deemed distribution of cash that triggers gain only in excess of basis.

why.A: Her share of the debt decrease is 30% x $60,000 = $18,000, a deemed cash distribution. It exceeds her basis of $10,000 by $8,000, which is gain.
why.B: Reports her basis as the gain.
why.C: Treats the whole deemed distribution as gain. Basis is recovered first.
why.D: Uses the whole loan repayment instead of her 30% share.

items.stem: Ari Volk owns 30% of the profits of a partnership. He also owns a building that he rents to the partnership for $24,000 a year at a fair rent. The partnership's 2026 ordinary income before deducting the rent is $200,000. How much total income does Ari report from the partnership and the rent?
items.rule_line: Payments to a partner in a non-partner capacity are treated as between the partnership and an outsider: deductible by the partnership and income to the partner.

why.A: Omits the rent Ari receives.
why.B: Ignores both the rent deduction and the rent income.
why.C: The rent is a payment to Ari acting other than as a partner, so it is deductible by the partnership and taxed to him as rent. His share of ordinary income is 30% x ($200,000 - $24,000) = $52,800. Total $76,800.
why.D: Adds the rent but fails to reduce the partnership's income for the rent it deducts.

items.task: Calculate a partner's tax realized and recognized gain (loss) on the contribution of noncash property to a partnership, and the partnership's basis in the property contributed.
items.stem: Ben Colby contributes land with an adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $90,000 to a partnership in which he has a 40% share of profits and Dee has a 60% share. The partnership later sells the land for $150,000. How much of the gain on the sale is allocated to Ben?
items.rule_line: Built-in gain on contributed property is allocated to the contributing partner; post-contribution gain is shared according to the partnership agreement.

why.A: Shares the whole gain by profit percentage and ignores that the built-in gain belongs to the contributor.
why.B: Allocates only the built-in gain and omits his share of the later appreciation.
why.C: The built-in gain at contribution, $90,000 - $30,000 = $60,000, is allocated to Ben. The remaining gain of $150,000 - $90,000 = $60,000 is shared 40% to Ben, giving him $24,000. Total $84,000.
why.D: Allocates the entire gain to Ben.

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a partner and a partnership
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a partnership and partners on a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property, and the partner's basis in the property received.
items.stem: Hal Kirk has an outside basis of $40,000 in his partnership interest. In a current (nonliquidating) distribution the partnership distributes to him marketable securities with a fair market value of $60,000 and a partnership basis of $35,000, and no other property. The partnership is not an investment partnership, Hal did not contribute the securities, and his share of net appreciation in the partnership's marketable securities immediately before the distribution is $0. What gain does Hal recognize?
items.rule_line: Marketable securities distributed by a partnership are treated as money, so gain arises to the extent their value exceeds the partner's outside basis.

why.A: Assumes a property distribution is tax-free within basis. Marketable securities are treated as cash for this purpose.
why.B: Marketable securities distributed are treated as money to the extent of their fair market value. The $60,000 deemed cash exceeds his outside basis of $40,000, so he recognizes gain of $20,000.
why.C: Measures gain against the partnership's basis in the securities instead of his outside basis.
why.D: Treats the whole value of the securities as gain and ignores his outside basis.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Nonliquidating distribution / Application

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a partner and a partnership
items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a partnership and partners on a liquidating distribution, and the partner's basis in the property received.
items.stem: Sue Mott liquidates her entire partnership interest, in which her basis is $60,000. She receives $20,000 in cash, inventory with a partnership basis of $15,000 (fair market value $30,000), and land with a partnership basis of $10,000 (fair market value $50,000). There is no change in liabilities. What is her basis in the land?
items.rule_line: In a liquidating distribution outside basis is reduced by cash, allocated first to inventory and receivables at carryover basis, then to other property.

why.A: Uses the partnership's basis in the land. In a liquidation, any remaining outside basis is assigned to the remaining property.
why.B: Also subtracts the land's own basis.
why.C: Splits the remaining basis equally between inventory and land.
why.D: In a liquidation the partner's outside basis is first reduced by cash ($20,000), then assigned to inventory at the partnership's basis ($15,000), and the remainder goes to the other property: $60,000 - $20,000 - $15,000 = $25,000.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Liquidating distribution / Application

items.task: Calculate the allocation of partnership income (loss) after the sale of a partner's share in a partnership for tax purposes.
items.stem: Eva Lin owned 40% of a calendar-year partnership until September 30, 2026, when she sold half of her interest, leaving her with a 20% interest. The partnership earned $300,000 of ordinary income ratably during 2026, and the partners agreed to allocate by proration. What is Eva's distributive share of the 2026 income?
items.rule_line: When a partner's interest varies during the year, distributive share is determined by the portion of the year each interest was held.

why.A: Uses 20% for the whole year. She held 40% for most of it.
why.B: Reverses the two ownership percentages.
why.C: Counts only the first nine months at 40%.
why.D: For the first nine months she held 40%: $300,000 x 9/12 x 40% = $90,000. For the last three months she held 20%: $300,000 x 3/12 x 20% = $15,000. Total $105,000.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Income allocation after sale / Application

items.task: Calculate the revised basis of partnership assets due to a transfer of a partnership interest for tax purposes.
items.stem: Gus Amato buys a 25% partnership interest from another partner for $150,000. The partnership's assets have a total inside basis of $400,000 and include land with a basis of $100,000 and a fair market value of $300,000. The other assets have a fair market value equal to their basis. Immediately after Gus's purchase the partnership sells the land for $300,000. By how much does an election to adjust the basis of partnership assets on transfers, in effect at the time of the purchase, reduce the gain Gus reports from the sale?
items.rule_line: A section 754 election gives a purchasing partner an inside basis adjustment equal to outside basis minus share of inside basis, allocated to appreciated assets.

why.A: Uses half of his share of the gain. The adjustment fully offsets his share here.
why.B: Without the election, Gus reports his 25% share of the partnership's $200,000 gain, or $50,000. With the election, the section 743(b) adjustment of $150,000 - (25% x $400,000) = $50,000 is allocated to the land, which eliminates that gain. The reduction is $50,000.
why.C: This is his share of inside basis, not the adjustment.
why.D: Uses the purchase price, which is not the basis adjustment.

steps: Gain without election = 25% x $200,000 = $50,000; with election = $0
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Basis adjustment on transfer / Analysis

items.task: Recall partner elections applicable to a partnership for tax purposes (e.g., partnership tax year, adjustment to basis of property).
items.stem: Which statement about the partnership election to adjust the basis of partnership property on transfers of interests is correct?
options: It is made separately by each transferee partner on a Form 8832 filed with the partnership's return each year
It applies only to the year in which it is made and must be made again with the return each year to continue
It applies only to transfers of interests at death and not to sales of interests or to partnership distributions
Once made, it applies to later transfers and to distributions until the IRS consents to revoke it
items.rule_line: A section 754 election is made by the partnership on a timely return and applies to transfers of interests and distributions in that and all later years.

why.A: The election is made by the partnership, not by an individual partner, and Form 8832 is an entity classification election.
why.B: The election continues to apply to later years until revoked with IRS consent.
why.C: The election also applies to sales and to certain distributions.
why.D: The election is made by the partnership with a timely filed return and stays in effect for all later transfers and distributions.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Partnership elections / Remembering & Understanding

items.subgroup_name: Transactions between a partner and a partnership
items.task: Calculate the tax implications of certain transactions between a partner and partnership (e.g., services performed by a partner) for tax purposes.
items.stem: Vera Muñoz owns 60% of the capital and profits of Marlow Partners. She sells land that she held as an investment (basis $40,000) to the partnership for $100,000, its fair market value. The partnership will hold the land as inventory for resale. What is the amount and character of Vera's gain?
options: $60,000 of ordinary income
$60,000 of long-term capital gain
$60,000 of section 1231 gain
$100,000 of ordinary income
items.rule_line: Gain on a sale of property between a partnership and a more-than-50% partner is ordinary if the property is not a capital asset to the transferee.

why.A: A gain on a sale between a partnership and a partner owning more than 50% is ordinary if the property is not a capital asset in the partnership's hands. The gain is $100,000 - $40,000 = $60,000, ordinary.
why.B: Would apply if the partnership held the land as a capital asset. Here it holds it as inventory.
why.C: Section 1231 does not apply because the property is inventory to the buyer, so the ordinary character rule controls.
why.D: Treats the whole price as ordinary income. Only the gain is income.

steps: Character: ordinary because the partnership holds the land as inventory

items.task: Recall and explain the characteristics of various types of trusts, including simple trusts, complex trusts and grantor trusts.
items.stem: The Wren Family Trust files a 2026 Form 1041. Which set of facts makes it a simple trust for 2026? The trust makes no charitable payments in any of the cases.
options: The trustee may accumulate income or distribute it to beneficiaries at the trustee's discretion
The trust instrument requires all income to be distributed currently, and no principal is distributed during the year
The instrument requires all income to be distributed currently, and the trustee also distributes $10,000 of principal to a beneficiary during the year
The grantor retains the power to revoke the trust, and all income is distributed currently to the beneficiary
items.rule_line: A simple trust must distribute all income currently, make no principal or charitable distributions, and not be a grantor trust; otherwise it is complex or grantor.

why.A: A trust that may accumulate income is a complex trust.
why.B: A simple trust must distribute all income currently, may not make principal distributions or charitable payments, and is not a grantor trust.
why.C: A trust that distributes principal in the year is a complex trust for that year.
why.D: A trust the grantor can revoke is a grantor trust, whose income is reported by the grantor rather than as a simple trust.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group D / Trust types / Application

items.task: Recall and explain a trust as a pass-through entity and the roles of grantor, trustee, and beneficiaries and the concept of corpus.
items.stem: Which statement about the taxation of a trust's income that is distributed to beneficiaries is correct?
options: The trust deducts every distribution it makes, including distributions of principal beyond distributable net income
The trust pays tax on all of its income, and beneficiaries exclude distributions from income as gifts
The trust deducts distributions up to distributable net income, and beneficiaries include them in income
The beneficiaries are taxed only on distributions in excess of distributable net income
items.rule_line: A trust is a conduit to the extent of DNI: it deducts distributions up to DNI and beneficiaries include them, retaining the character of the income.

why.A: The distribution deduction cannot exceed distributable net income.
why.B: Distributions of income are taxed to the beneficiaries to the extent of distributable net income and are not gifts.
why.C: The distribution deduction is limited to DNI, which also limits what beneficiaries include in income.
why.D: The opposite is true: distributions up to DNI are taxed to the beneficiaries; the excess is not.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group D / Trust as pass-through / Remembering & Understanding

items.task: Recall and explain the characteristics of revocable trusts.
items.stem: Carol Reed created a trust in 2020 and transferred property to it. She kept the power to revoke the trust and to withdraw the assets at any time. Which statement about the trust in 2026 is correct?
options: The trust is a separate taxpayer that files its own return and takes a personal exemption of $300 a year
The transfer to the trust was a completed gift when made and is subject to federal gift tax at that time
The trust assets are excluded from Carol's gross estate because legal title is held by an independent trustee
Its income is taxed to Carol, and its assets are in her gross estate if she dies while it is revocable
items.rule_line: A revocable trust is a grantor trust: the grantor reports its income, the transfer is an incomplete gift, and the assets are in the gross estate.

why.A: A revocable trust is disregarded as a separate taxpayer; the grantor reports the income.
why.B: Because Carol kept the power to revoke, the transfer was not a completed gift.
why.C: Legal title does not matter. The retained power to revoke causes estate inclusion.
why.D: A revocable trust is a grantor trust, so its income is taxed to the grantor, and the retained power to revoke brings the assets into the estate.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group D / Revocable trusts / Remembering & Understanding

items.task: Identify the allocation of items between income and corpus in a given scenario.
items.stem: The Hollis Trust received $12,000 of cash dividends and $5,000 of interest in 2026 and sold stock at a $30,000 gain. It paid $3,000 of regular trustee compensation. Assume the state has adopted the Uniform Principal and Income Act: cash dividends and interest are income, capital gains are principal, and regular trustee compensation is charged half to income and half to principal. What is the trust's fiduciary accounting income for 2026?
items.rule_line: Fiduciary accounting income includes dividends and interest, excludes capital gains, and is reduced by expenses charged to income under state law.

why.A: Counts only the interest and leaves out the dividends.
why.B: Counts only the dividends and leaves out the interest.
why.C: Charges all of the trustee compensation to income, but only half is charged to income.
why.D: Income consists of dividends and interest ($17,000) less half of the trustee compensation charged to income ($1,500): $15,500. The capital gain is principal.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group D / Income/corpus allocation / Application

items.task: Calculate a trust's accounting income, distributable net income and taxable income, including the income distribution deduction.
items.stem: The Marsh Trust is a complex trust. In 2026 it had $20,000 of dividends and $10,000 of interest, and a $15,000 capital gain that the trustee allocated to corpus and retained. It paid $4,000 of trustee fees, all charged to income and deductible. The trustee distributed $20,000 that the instrument required to Ann and $10,000 in a discretionary distribution to Bill. The trust's exemption is $100. What is the trust's 2026 taxable income?
items.rule_line: A trust's taxable income equals its income less deductions, the distribution deduction (limited to DNI), and its exemption.

why.A: Deducts the full distributions. The deduction is limited to distributable net income.
why.B: Distributable net income is $20,000 + $10,000 - $4,000 = $26,000; the corpus capital gain is excluded. The distributions ($30,000) exceed DNI, so the deduction is $26,000. Taxable income = $41,000 - $26,000 - $100 = $14,900.
why.C: Leaves out the trust's $100 exemption.
why.D: Takes no distribution deduction at all.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group D / Trust DNI/taxable income / Application

items.task: Calculate a trust's accounting income, distributable net income and taxable income, including the income distribution deduction.
items.stem: The Vale Trust has $60,000 of taxable income before any distribution deduction and exemption. Assume the trust's tax is $3,000 on the first $16,000 of income and 37% on the rest if it keeps the income. The trust's sole beneficiary is in the 24% bracket. The trustee can either retain the income or distribute all of it currently; distributable net income equals $60,000. Ignoring the trust exemption, what federal income tax does the family save by distributing the income?
items.rule_line: Distributing income carries it out to beneficiaries, often at lower rates than the compressed trust brackets.

why.A: If the trust retains the income it pays $3,000 + 37% x ($60,000 - $16,000) = $19,280. If it distributes all income, the beneficiary pays 24% x $60,000 = $14,400 and the trust owes nothing. The saving is $4,880.
why.B: Assumes all retained income is taxed at 37%. The first $16,000 is taxed at lower amounts.
why.C: This is the beneficiary's tax on the distribution, not the saving.
why.D: This is the trust's tax if it keeps the income, not the saving.

items.law_note: The trust tax figures are stem assumptions. The actual 2026 trust schedule (Rev. Proc. 2025-32) is $3,851 plus 37% over $16,000; the answer's logic is unchanged.
